title: Percentages, fractions and ratio strengths (% w/v, 1 in 1,000)
blurb: Turn % w/v and "1 in" ratio strengths into grams, milligrams and micrograms per mL, and work out percentages of a dose.
question: Lidocaine 1% w/v is drawn up for a perineal repair. How many milligrams are in 8 mL?

teach.h: Strength written as a percentage or a ratio
teach.body: % w/v (weight in volume) means grams of drug in every 100 mL. So 5% w/v glucose is 5 g in 100 mL. A ratio strength "1 in 1,000" means 1 g in 1000 mL. Plain English: both are just another way of writing a concentration, and once you turn them into mg per mL the usual dose arithmetic applies. Part A practice papers did not show these items, so treat them as stretch practice.
teach.cite: FACTS section 4: percentage and ratio strengths

teach.body: A percentage is a number out of 100. To find 15% of 60 mg: 60 x 15 ÷ 100 = 9 mg. To reduce a dose by 25%, keep 75%: 800 x 0.75 = 600 mg. To increase by 10%, multiply by 1.1.

items: Midwife Aisha Begum draws up 8 mL of lidocaine 1% w/v for a perineal repair.
1% w/v = 1 g in 100 mL = 1000 mg in 100 mL = 10 mg in each mL.
Sense check with the shortcut: 1% x 10 = 10 mg/mL; 8 mL holds 80 mg.
Any maximum dose in the question is then compared with 80 mg.

teach.caption: One extra zero in the ratio means the solution is ten times weaker.

teach.text: Confusing 1 in 1,000 with 1 in 10,000 is a tenfold error. And % w/v is grams per 100 mL, not per 1 mL: 5% glucose is 50 mg per mL, not 5 g per mL.

items.label: = mg per mL for any % w/v

items: % w/v = grams in 100 mL; mg per mL = % x 10.
1 in 1,000 = 1 mg per mL; 1 in 10,000 = 0.1 mg per mL.
Each extra zero in a ratio makes it ten times weaker.
x% of a quantity = quantity x x ÷ 100.
Convert the strength to mg per mL, then use your usual formula.

summary: You can now decode % w/v and "1 in" ratio strengths into an amount per mL, find the amount in a given volume, and calculate percentages and percentage reductions of a dose.

A.q: Glucose 5% w/v contains 5 g in every 100 mL. How many grams of glucose are in 250 mL?
A.why: 250 mL is 2.5 lots of 100 mL. 2.5 x 5 g = 12.5 g.

whyNot.0: Tenfold error: 2.5 x 5 g is 12.5 g.
whyNot.1: Tenfold error the other way: 250 mL is 2.5 lots of 100 mL.
whyNot.2: This is the amount in 1000 mL, not 250 mL.

A.q: Sodium chloride 0.45% w/v contains 0.45 g in every 100 mL. How many grams of sodium chloride are in 1 L?

whyNot.0: This is the amount in 100 mL; 1 L is ten times more.
whyNot.2: Hundredfold error: 1000 mL is 10 lots of 100 mL.

A.q: Adrenaline 1 in 10,000 means 1 g in 10,000 mL. How many milligrams are in each 1 mL?

whyNot.1: This is the strength of 1 in 1,000.
whyNot.3: Inverted the ratio: 10000 mL ÷ 1000 mg gives mL per mg, not mg per mL.

B.q: A midwife draws up 8 mL of lidocaine 1% w/v (1 g in every 100 mL) for a perineal repair. How many milligrams of lidocaine are in 8 mL?
B.why: 1% = 1000 mg in 100 mL = 10 mg per mL. 8 x 10 = 80 mg.

whyNot.0: Used 1 mg per mL; 1% is 10 mg per mL.
whyNot.1: Used 100 mg per mL; that is a 10% solution.
whyNot.3: Used 0.1 mg per mL; 1% is 10 mg per mL.

B.q: An adult on a medical ward receives 2 L of glucose 5% w/v (5 g in every 100 mL) over 24 hours. How many grams of glucose is this?

whyNot.0: This is the amount in 200 mL; 2 L is 20 lots of 100 mL.
whyNot.2: Tenfold error: 20 x 5 g is 100 g.
whyNot.3: This is the amount in 100 mL.

B.q: A dose of 800 mg is to be reduced by 25%. What is the new dose?

whyNot.0: This is the reduction itself, not the new dose.

C.q: An adult needs adrenaline 500 micrograms IM. The ampoule is 1 in 1,000 (1 g in 1,000 mL). What volume is needed? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: 1 in 1,000 = 1 mg per mL. 500 micrograms = 0.5 mg. 0.5 ÷ 1 x 1 mL = 0.5 mL.

whyNot.0: Used the 1 in 10,000 strength (0.1 mg per mL).
whyNot.1: Tenfold error: 500 micrograms is 0.5 mg, which is 0.5 mL.
whyNot.2: Divided 500 micrograms by 1 mg per mL without converting micrograms to mg.

C.q: A woman needs magnesium sulfate 4 g. The ampoules are 50% w/v (50 g in every 100 mL). What volume contains 4 g?

whyNot.0: Tenfold error: 50% is 0.5 g per mL.
whyNot.2: Tenfold error the other way: 4 ÷ 0.5 is 8.

C.q: Lidocaine with adrenaline contains adrenaline 1 in 200,000 (1 g in 200,000 mL). How many micrograms of adrenaline are in each 1 mL?

whyNot.2: Inverted the ratio instead of dividing 1 g by 200,000 mL.

reteach.title: Percent means per hundred
reteach.question: If 2% w/v means 2 g in 100 mL, how much is in 1 mL?

blocks.body: Every % w/v tells you grams in 100 mL. Divide by 100 to get grams per mL, then x 1000 for mg per mL. Together that is x 10: 2% = 20 mg per mL, 0.9% = 9 mg per mL.

blocks.text: Ratios get weaker as the number gets bigger: 1 in 10,000 is weaker than 1 in 1,000.

explain.body: 10% w/v = 10 g in 100 mL = 10000 mg in 100 mL = 100 mg per mL.

test.q: A solution is 10% w/v (10 g in every 100 mL). How many milligrams are in each 1 mL?

whyNot.1: This is the strength of 1% w/v.
whyNot.2: This is the amount in 10 mL.
whyNot.3: This is grams per mL (10 g ÷ 100 mL = 0.1 g); it has not been converted to mg.

explain.body: x% of a quantity = quantity x x ÷ 100.

whyNot.0: Divided 60 by 15 instead of taking 15 per 100.
whyNot.3: This is 60 mg reduced by 15%, not 15% of it.

explain.body: 1 g in 1000 mL = 1000 mg in 1000 mL = 1 mg per mL = 1000 micrograms per mL.

test.q: Adrenaline 1 in 1,000 (1 g in 1,000 mL) is drawn up. How many micrograms are in 0.3 mL?
test.why: 1000 micrograms per mL x 0.3 mL = 300 micrograms.

whyNot.0: Used 100 micrograms per mL, the 1 in 10,000 strength.
whyNot.3: Gave the volume as the amount; 1 mL holds 1000 micrograms.

explain.text: One extra zero in the ratio makes the solution ten times weaker, so you need ten times the volume.

test.q: Adrenaline 1 in 10,000 (1 g in 10,000 mL) is available. What volume contains 1 mg?

whyNot.1: This is the volume for the 1 in 1,000 strength.
whyNot.2: Multiplied 1 mg by 0.1 mg per mL instead of dividing.
whyNot.3: This would be the volume for a 1 in 100,000 strength.
